question: Who started the first Topographical Survey in India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Major James Rennel**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Major James Rennell is known as the "Father of the Indian Survey" and is credited with starting the first topographical survey in India.
 
• He was an English geographer, historian, and oceanography pioneer. He was appointed as the first Surveyor General of India in 1767.
 
• Rennell's cartographic surveys were a turning point in the scale and importance of cartography in India.
 
• His work included accurate maps of Bengal and outlines of India.
 
• His work inspired a generation of surveyors and cartographers for the Company.
 
• His surveys were the foundation for the Survey of India, which eventually employed nearly 150 Europeans and a large number of native surveyors.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• William Lambton:
 
 
• William Lambton was a British geographer and surveyor who initiated the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India in 1802.
 
• His work laid the foundation for the precise mapping of the Indian subcontinent, including the measurement of the meridian arc from the southern tip of India to the Himalayas.
 
 
 
• Col. Alexander Read:
 
 
• Col. Alexander Read was a British military officer and administrator known for his role in developing the Ryotwari system in parts of southern India.
 
• This system allowed direct collection of land revenue from the peasants (ryots), and it influenced the subsequent revenue models adopted in British India.
 
 
 
• Nain Singh:
 
 
• Nain Singh was a renowned Indian explorer and surveyor who worked for the British Survey of India in the 19th century.
 
• He is famous for his pioneering explorations of Tibet and Central Asia, mapping the previously uncharted regions and determining the location and altitude of Lhasa, Tibet's capital.
